entries.clue: Sumerian translated in S American country (8)

indicatorNotes.translated: translating turns words into new forms, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: An ancient Sumerian text being rendered into a language spoken in South America.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a note about an ancient tablet, yet 'Sumerian' is not a language to translate but a set of letters, and they rearrange exactly into the country.
annotation.definitionFit: Suriname is a small country on the north-east coast of South America.

entries.clue: Now quiet, in the main, getting mangetout (4,4)

indicatorNotes.in: the new pieces go in the word for the main

blocks.note: the main = the open sea; SEAS holds NOW + P

annotation.surface: A sailor, now calm at sea, finally getting fresh greens on board.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The main' is an old word for the open sea, as in the Spanish Main. Mangetout is the British name for flat pea pods eaten whole.
annotation.definitionFit: Mangetout and snow peas are two names for the same flat edible pea pods.

entries.clue: Concerning, uncompromising stint (8)

blocks.note: re = concerning, as in memo headers

annotation.surface: Someone describing a hard, unbending spell of duty.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stint' looks like a noun, a period of work, but it is the verb: to stint is to hold back or limit.
annotation.definitionFit: To stint on something is to restrict it, keeping supply short.

entries.clue: Beaks pointing up, two sons touring Spain (5)

indicatorNotes.pointing up: in a down entry, pointing up means read from the bottom
indicatorNotes.touring: the sons travel round Spain, so they surround it

blocks.note: E = Spain, its international vehicle code
the second son spelt in full; S + SON go round E to make SESON

annotation.surface: Birds with upturned bills, or two lads on a trip around Spain.
annotation.walkthrough: The two sons are given differently, one as S and one as SON. Beak is slang for a nose.
annotation.definitionFit: Beak is informal for a person's nose, so beaks are noses.

entries.clue: Glibness, to the crossword compiler? Not entirely good news! (5,8)

blocks.note: to a setter any word is a bag of letters, and these eight rearrange into a word for a boon
the straight reading: something welcome that comes with a drawback

annotation.surface: A remark that a smooth talker's glibness is not wholly welcome news.
annotation.walkthrough: The joke is that a setter sees any word as possible letters: GLIBNESS is literally a mixed BLESSING. The second half then gives the phrase its everyday sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A mixed blessing is something with both advantages and drawbacks, so not entirely good.

entries.clue: Do mountain activity: muscles ache, you say? (6)

indicatorNotes.you say: points to how the words sound when spoken

annotation.surface: A climber complaining of sore stomach muscles after a day on the rocks.
annotation.walkthrough: Aching abs is exactly how you feel after a day on the ropes, so the pun fits the scene.
annotation.definitionFit: To abseil is to descend a rock face on a rope, a mountaineering activity.

entries.clue: Fathead suggests this vegetable (5,4)

blocks.note: the fat part: fat = broad, wide
the head part: bean = head, informal

annotation.surface: Calling someone a fathead, as if the insult pointed to a vegetable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fathead' reads as one insult but splits into FAT and HEAD. Bean for head is old slang, as in 'use your bean'.
annotation.definitionFit: The broad bean is a large flat green bean eaten as a vegetable.

entries.clue: Derive conclusion in knowledge (lawful) (6)

indicatorNotes.conclusion in: the conclusion of a word is its last letter

annotation.surface: A reasoner drawing a conclusion from what they know, while staying within the law.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Derive conclusion' reads as one phrase about logic, but 'conclusion' belongs to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: To elicit is to draw out or derive a response or piece of information.

entries.clue: Gets free fires (4,2)

annotation.surface: Someone escaping from burning buildings.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fires' looks like flames, but it is the verb: to fire someone is to let them go.
annotation.definitionFit: To let go means both to release something and to dismiss an employee.

entries.clue: Some neuropsychiatric medical procedures (3)

indicatorNotes.Some: only part of the next word is used

annotation.surface: Brain operations carried out by psychiatric doctors.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all hospital, so the answer sits right in the scene; only the long word hides it.
annotation.definitionFit: Ops is short for operations, which are medical procedures.

entries.clue: One with horn, aroused, has options including kiss (11)

indicatorNotes.aroused: stirred up, so the letters are jumbled
indicatorNotes.including: the kiss goes in with the other letters

blocks.note: X = a kiss, as at the end of a letter

annotation.surface: A cheeky line about a randy person weighing up whom to kiss.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is saucy on purpose: 'horn' and 'aroused' point one way, while 'horn' is a jazz word for a saxophone.
annotation.definitionFit: Jazz players call any wind instrument, especially a saxophone, a horn, so a saxophonist is one with a horn.

entries.clue: Wearing Armani, perhaps depressing row resolved (5,8)

indicatorNotes.resolved: a problem resolved is sorted out, so the letters are sorted anew

annotation.surface: A gloomy argument settled, with someone in designer clothes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' warns that Armani is just one example of the smart suits in question.
annotation.definitionFit: Power dressing is wearing sharp, expensive business clothes, such as Armani suits, to look authoritative.

entries.clue: Stated acidity level pulled down (7)

blocks.note: rased = razed, an old spelling for demolished

annotation.surface: A report that the acidity level has been brought down.
annotation.walkthrough: RASED is a less common spelling of razed, meaning a building pulled down to the ground.
annotation.definitionFit: Something phrased has been put into words, that is, stated.

entries.clue: Losing three at outset: longwinded, rambling, where speeches made … (7)

indicatorNotes.Losing three at outset: the first three letters are dropped
indicatorNotes.rambling: wandering about, so the letters move

blocks.note: LONGWINDED minus its first three letters, LON

annotation.surface: A grumble about long, rambling speeches at a function, running on into the next clue.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface complains about speeches, and a wedding is exactly where the long-winded ones happen. The dots carry the sentence into 14 across.
annotation.definitionFit: A wedding reception is the classic occasion for speeches.

entries.clue: … open bar, components swapped, causing no intoxication (7-4)

indicatorNotes.components swapped: the two parts of the phrase change places

blocks.note: an open bar serves free alcohol; the swap puts ALCOHOL first

annotation.surface: Continuing the wedding: a free bar, yet somehow nobody gets drunk.
annotation.walkthrough: An open bar means FREE ALCOHOL; swapping the two words gives the answer, the opposite of what an open bar promises.
annotation.definitionFit: Alcohol-free drinks contain no alcohol, so they cause no intoxication.

entries.clue: Obstructing picnic provisions on island: no good! (9)

blocks.note: a hamper is a basket of picnic food

annotation.surface: A disappointing picnic on an island.
annotation.walkthrough: A hamper is a lidded wicker basket packed with picnic food, familiar in Britain.
annotation.definitionFit: To hamper is to hinder or obstruct, so hampering is obstructing.

entries.clue: After very boastful statement, National Theatre highly malignant (8)

annotation.surface: A bitter review of the National Theatre after it boasted about itself.
annotation.walkthrough: The National Theatre is the national theatre company of Britain, based in London.
annotation.definitionFit: Virulent describes a disease that is extremely severe or harmful, highly malignant.

entries.clue: Bits of Lego I stick together, self-absorbed (8)

indicatorNotes.Bits of: the answer is made of pieces of the words that follow
indicatorNotes.stick together: those pieces join into one run

annotation.surface: A child snapping plastic bricks together, lost in their own world.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stick together' is exactly what Lego bricks do, so the instruction hides as a description of play. LEGO even carries EGO.
annotation.definitionFit: Egoistic means self-centred, absorbed in oneself.

entries.clue: Mr Farah, running fast? Only if this has happened! (11)

annotation.definition: Mr Farah, running fast? Only if this has happened!

blocks.note: reads as a sports line about the Olympic distance runner, whose first name is Mo, not Mr
the setter admits the name is wrong: a letter has been set in error

annotation.surface: A sports report on the runner Mo Farah, which has gone oddly wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: Mo Farah is a British Olympic distance champion. MO SPRINTING, with one letter changed, spells the answer, and 'Mr' for Mo is itself one.
annotation.definitionFit: The clue only makes sense if a misprint has happened, turning Mo into Mr.

entries.clue: First goal that allows Reds breathing space? (6)

blocks.note: the goal that opens the scoring in a match
red wines are uncorked to breathe, and a bottle tool lets them

annotation.surface: A football report: the Reds relax after scoring first.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reds' looks like the nickname of Liverpool or Manchester United, football clubs that play in red, but it means red wines, which are opened to let them breathe.
annotation.definitionFit: An opener is both the first goal of a game and a bottle opener, the tool that lets wine breathe.

entries.clue: TV controller’s heading off: makes song and dance (6)

indicatorNotes.heading off: the head, the first letter, comes off

blocks.note: REMOTE'S without its first letter R

annotation.surface: Someone with the TV remote in hand leaves and makes a scene.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heading off' reads as someone leaving; it means the first letter goes.
annotation.definitionFit: To make a song and dance is to make a showy fuss, as one who emotes does.

entries.clue: Preserved over millennia – pumice erupted – immortally Italian, primarily? (7)

annotation.definition: Preserved over millennia – pumice erupted – immortally Italian, primarily?

indicatorNotes.primarily: take what comes first in each word

blocks.clueFragment: Preserved over millennia – pumice erupted – immortally Italian
blocks.note: the first letters of Preserved Over Millennia Pumice Erupted Immortally Italian

annotation.surface: A description of a Roman city buried under volcanic ash and kept for ever.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the letters and a description of the place: Pompeii was buried by Vesuvius in AD 79 and preserved under pumice and ash.
annotation.definitionFit: Pompeii is the Italian city preserved for nearly two millennia by the eruption of Vesuvius.

entries.clue: With one student, university (MIT)’s flipping offering incentives (7)

indicatorNotes.flipping: flipped over, so the whole run reads backwards

annotation.surface: An American university offering rewards to attract a student.
annotation.walkthrough: L for student comes from the learner plates on British cars. The possessive 's supplies its S too.
annotation.definitionFit: Stimuli are things that spur action, which is what incentives are.

entries.clue: Everyman’s ‘grand bathroom’? Freezing, rudimentary place (5)

blocks.note: the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as I

annotation.surface: The setter joking about a cold, basic lavatory.
annotation.walkthrough: A setter's name in a clue usually stands for I or ME. Loo is everyday British for a toilet.
annotation.definitionFit: An igloo is a simple dome shelter of snow blocks, a freezing, basic dwelling.

entries.clue: Not initially tying up driver Damon somewhere in London (7,4)

indicatorNotes.Not initially: the first letter is not there

blocks.note: KNOTTING (tying up) without its first letter K
Damon Hill, Formula One world champion

annotation.surface: A racing driver being tied up, or not.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not' wants to be a word in the answer, and NOT does appear, but only because KNOTTING loses its K. Notting Hill is a district of west London.
annotation.definitionFit: Notting Hill is an area of west London, famous for its carnival.

entries.clue: Consume with passion in East End (3)

indicatorNotes.in East End: Cockneys of London's East End drop their Hs

annotation.surface: Eating eagerly somewhere in east London.
annotation.walkthrough: In the East End of London the Cockney accent drops the H, so heat becomes 'eat.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: consuming a meal and eating it are the same act.

entries.clue: Once more endorse – or call it a day? (6)

annotation.surface: A player weighing a new contract against retiring.
annotation.walkthrough: The two senses are pronounced differently: re-SIGN with a hard S, and re-ZINE for quitting.
annotation.definitionFit: To resign is to give up a job, calling it a day; to re-sign is to sign again.

entries.clue: Coasting, out of control? I’m not sure (8)

annotation.surface: A driver freewheeling downhill and unsure whether they still have control.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I'm not sure' reads as the driver's worry, but it is what an agnostic says about God.
annotation.definitionFit: An agnostic holds that they cannot be sure whether God exists.
